1:
What the boy actually did is filled in from outside the text. Gill has him opening and shutting the doors of the tabernacle, lighting the lamps and singing praises, and reports from Josephus that he was then about twelve; Clarke agrees that these were minor services performed under Eli's direction. Ellicott is struck by how little is said: the writer knew this prophet second only to Moses in his influence, yet gives the shortest possible account of his childhood. What it does establish, he thinks, is the purity of the atmosphere — the boy was kept from the party of Hophni and Phinehas, and the old priest, perhaps taught wisdom by his own headstrong sons, watched over his charge with care. Ellicott sets the two side by side: the grown men prostituted the holy work to their own worldly ends while the child ministered before the Lord in his little white robe. Henry draws the same contrast as a rebuke, that it aggravated the wickedness of Eli's sons to be shamed by a child, and turns it into counsel — he who was faithful in a little was soon entrusted with more, so let the young be humble and diligent, since those are fittest to rule who have learnt to obey.

That the word of the Lord was precious is taken by three of them to mean simply that it was scarce, each deriving the value from the scarcity. Wesley puts it most bluntly, that rare things are most precious in men's esteem while common things are generally despised; Henry allows that the rarity made it more precious to those who knew how to put a right value on it; Clarke says that because the word was scarce it was therefore valuable. Clarke then draws an inference about the writer rather than the age described: the man who recorded this probably lived when prophecy was frequent. On open vision they agree again — there was no accredited prophet with whom the secret of the Lord was known to dwell, to whom any might resort in doubt or emergency — though Wesley qualifies it, that God might still reveal himself privately to pious persons. Wesley alone says why the notice stands where it does: it is premised as the reason Samuel did not understand when God called him the first time and the second.

Keil reads the opening as grammar. Verses two to four form a single period, the clause about that time being resumed only at the words that the Lord called, everything between being circumstantial clauses put in to light up the situation. On that reading the dimness of Eli's eyes is not a detail about Eli but a device for explaining Samuel: hearing his own name called in the night, the boy would naturally suppose that the old man who could no longer see was calling for help. Keil also defends a rare construction against those who would emend it, finding it supported elsewhere.

The lamp is dated and then allegorised. Keil identifies it as the candlestick, whose seven lamps were lit every evening to burn through the night; Clarke takes the note to mean before sunrise, since the lamps were extinguished before the sun rose; Wesley says the same in one line. Gill adds that some usually went out by morning while the western lamp never did, then reports a reading of another kind: some understand the lamp of prophecy, so that before it was quite extinct in Eli the spirit of prophecy came upon Samuel — as the Jews express it, before one sun was set another arose, as before the sun of Moses set the sun of Joshua arose. Clarke ends with the architecture, supposing that since the ark had been long at Shiloh they had built apartments nearby, and that Samuel lay in one close to Eli's, perhaps under the same roof.
4:
Where the voice came from is answered by position. Gill has it issuing from the most holy place, from between the cherubim; Clarke supposes it came from the holy place near which both Eli and Samuel were lying. Gill also supplies the boy's motive for running, that he dressed and hurried as fast as he could because he supposed the old man needed help, and made the more haste out of affection, knowing his age and infirmities.

Why Samuel did not recognise the voice is treated as a question about what he lacked. Gill insists it was not ignorance of God: he knew Jehovah as the true God and had been instructed by Eli in his word and worship. The Targum makes it a want of doctrine, which Gill will accept only as imperfection in a child. The real sense, he says after Maimonides, is that Samuel did not know that God had ever spoken to men in an ordinary and familiar voice — he had perhaps never heard of such a thing, and so could not distinguish the voice of God from the voice of Eli. Clarke says the same more briefly, that he knew and worshipped the God of Israel but did not know him as one who communicated special revelations of his will. Wesley turns the deficiency into an advantage: the boy's ignorance served God's design, since his simplicity gave Eli the better assurance that the call was genuine.

Ellicott reconstructs the night as a scene, and remarks first on the telling — the story is so naturally told, the supernatural so interwoven with the common life of the sanctuary, that a reader forgets the strangeness of what is recorded. Then he supplies the conversation the text omits. He fancies the old man asking, when the boy came in a third time, where the voice he took for Eli's had come from, and the boy answering that it came from his master's chamber; and the high priest remembering that in that same direction, at the far end of the sanctuary behind the veil, stood the ark and the seat of God. Was the glory of the Lord shining there, and did the voice proceed from that golden throne as in the old days? So he sent his pupil back with instructions to answer not Eli but the invisible King. Clarke notes that the words he was told to use were the usual form among the prophets when they had intimation that God was about to reveal something.

The last approach divides them, and the division is about what kind of event this was. Keil fixes on the statement that the Lord came and stood, and takes it to prove the point at issue: these words show that the revelation was an objectively real affair and not a mere dream of Samuel's. The others explain the same words as an impression. Clarke supposes the boy heard the voice coming nearer and nearer until, from the sameness of its tone, he judged it had stopped approaching, and that this is what is represented under the notion of God standing. Wesley says the voice, which before had spoken at a distance from the oracle between the cherubim, now came near, as if the speaker were standing beside him — and that this was to prevent any further mistake. Gill offers three possibilities and prefers the third: a corporeal form seen in the vision of prophecy, as Kimchi held; or a bright splendour, an illustrious appearance of the glory of God; or, more probably, simply that the voice which had seemed to come from where Eli lay now sounded close in his ears.
11:
Henry begins with what the message is not. God did not come to tell the boy how great a man he would be; young people commonly have a curiosity to be told their fortune, and God came not to gratify it but to employ him and send him on an errand to somebody else. He also accounts for the message being shorter than the one the man of God had brought earlier: Samuel was a child and could not remember a long one, and God considered his frame — the memories of children must not be overcharged, not even with divine things. He adds that divine threatenings come the surer and fall the heavier for being disregarded, and that this errand might serve Samuel later, when his own sons proved not so good as they should have been.

What the tingling ears foretell is identified by Ellicott as the capture of the ark. Neither the death of the two priests nor the defeat of the army would have shaken the people so; that the sign of the invisible King's protection should fall into the hands of the uncircumcised was unparalleled in their annals, and seemed to say God had forsaken them. He notes the expression is very singular and recurs only of the destruction of Jerusalem. Clarke keeps to the figure and makes it an aftersound, a piercing word that goes on resounding once heard. He also argues from the boy's age against any vision: Samuel probably saw nothing, since it is unlikely any extraordinary representation was made to eyes so young.

The clause about beginning and making an end is read two ways. Clarke takes it to exclude delay: God will not put off his purpose, and once begun nothing shall deter him. Wesley takes it to allow a long delay and then exclude reprieve — the day appointed was twenty or thirty years off, so much space of repentance allowed a wicked generation, yet once begun the vengeance is not desisted from until a full end is made. Gill notes that the earlier prophecy preceded this message, against the sense of some, and that the oath was either sworn before or is sworn now to confirm it. Keil settles the Hebrew, that to judge a crime is simply to punish it, and that for ever means the punishment is never lifted.

On Eli's fault they agree about the fact and differ about its weight. Keil states it flatly: he knew his sons were bringing a curse upon themselves and did not prevent them. Clarke says he failed to use his parental and judicial authority to curb them. Wesley is severest, that Eli contented himself with a cold reproof instead of punishing, and draws a rule: those who can restrain others from sin and do not are partakers of the guilt, and men in authority have much to answer for if the sword they bear is no terror to evildoers. Ellicott measures the sin by the mischief it worked — the example set at Shiloh filtered through the people until unbelief was becoming general — and observes the high priest knew this and still would not remove his sons.

That no sacrifice can purge the iniquity draws the widest answers. Clarke restricts it: what is spoken relates to their temporal death only, since they had sinned unto death and no offering could avert a violent end. Wesley reads it as meaning the sentence cannot be bought off. Ellicott finds a great truth in the few words: the Mosaic system itself acknowledged a limit to the efficacy of sacrifice, a scar no blood of bullock or goat could wash away — and yet, from the resignation with which the old man afterwards received the sentence, he infers that Eli looked past it to some other deliverance, seeing as in a glass darkly the blood of another victim.
15:
Gill notices what the text does not say. It says Samuel lay until the morning, not that he slept, and Gill thinks he can hardly have slept, considering what had befallen him — the honour done to a child in being spoken to, and the dreadful things said of Eli's family — so that he lay musing until morning.

The doors he opened are turned into evidence about the building. Ellicott takes the notice as evidence that the sanctuary at Shiloh was enclosed in a house: no record survives of the building of the first house of the Lord, but the references here make it clear the tabernacle had for some time been enclosed by, and perhaps roofed over with, permanent structures. Wesley reasons identically — while the tabernacle travelled it had only curtains at the entrance, but once settled it was enclosed within some solid building with doors and posts. Both infer an architecture from one word.

Why the boy was afraid is answered three ways. Clarke observes something easy to miss, that it does not appear God had commanded Samuel to deliver the message at all, so he did not attempt it until adjured; and that he reverenced the old man as a father and feared to distress him. Wesley gives that reason and adds a second and shrewder one, that had Samuel been hasty to utter it, Eli might have thought him guilty of arrogance, or of a secret complacency in his calamity. Ellicott quotes another commentary: here was Samuel's first experience of the prophet's cross, having unwelcome truth to divulge to those he loved and honoured, a cross Jeremiah found exceedingly heavy. Clarke and Wesley alike read the adjuration as an imprecation — if you do not tell me fully, may the same curses and greater fall on you — and Gill explains Eli's urgency, that he had slighted the man of God who came before, so God took this method to convince him.

Eli's answer is where they are most nearly unanimous, and one is following another. Keil says that Eli bowed in quiet resignation, and that his reply proves that with all his weakness and criminal indulgence towards his wicked sons he was thoroughly devoted to the Lord in his heart. Ellicott says that the reply indicates that Eli, in spite of his weakness and foolish partiality for his sons, was thoroughly devoted to the Lord in his heart — the same judgment in almost the same words, and the earlier writer is Keil. Ellicott then goes further than his source, and darker: it was too late for reformation, the power of Hophni and Phinehas being too strong for an enfeebled will, so that Eli was in his last days little more than a puppet in their hands, having sown the wind and now obliged to reap the whirlwind. Clarke finds in the words much godly submission and a deep sense of unworthiness, and enters a caution: Eli had sinned so as to be punished with temporal death, but there is no evidence the Lord's displeasure extended to a future state. Wesley expands it into Eli's own reasoning, that the sentence comes from the sovereign Lord who has absolute right to dispose of all his creatures and is in a special manner ruler of Israel, whose chastisement he therefore accepts.

Keil turns the scene to Samuel's credit: by communicating without reserve so solemn a word against a man he venerated with filial affection, the boy proved he had courage to proclaim the word of the Lord without fear. Gill draws the rule that the whole counsel of God is to be declared and nothing concealed, whether it please men or not. Clarke pauses over the English rather than the Hebrew, deriving the word whit from the Anglo-Saxon for a person or thing, so that every whit is every thing.
19:
That Samuel grew is expanded in the usual directions — Gill takes it of grace, wisdom and reputation as well as stature, Clarke simply of increase to manhood — but Ellicott hears another comparison. Each brief notice about the boy, he thinks, is set against somebody: earlier against the sons of Eli, and here against Eli himself. The Lord was with his servant now as no doubt he had been with Eli in earlier days; what differs is that this young prophet let none of the divine words fall to the ground. In those dark days at Shiloh, amid scenes of temptation, the boy stood firm, and his early life was a perpetual protest against covetousness and iniquity. Henry draws the same growth back to its cause, that all our increase in wisdom and grace is owing to the presence of God with us, which is all in all to our growth.

The promise that no word fell to the ground is variously pictured and variously supported. Wesley finds a metaphor from precious liquors, which once spilt upon the ground are altogether useless. Keil collects the idiom from three other passages, where the same verb is used of a word God does not let fall. Henry supposes there were early instances of Samuel's predictions coming true, which confirmed those fulfilled later and satisfied the people about his mission; and takes the renewal of the visions for a rule, that God graciously repeats his visits to those who receive them aright.

On the word rendered established, Clarke and Keil converge from opposite traditions. Clarke says plainly that the Hebrew signifies faithful, so that the sentence means the faithful Samuel was a prophet of the Lord. Keil renders it found trustworthy or approved, and refers for the usage to the verse where Moses is called faithful in all God's house — which places the boy, by a single word, in the company of the man Ellicott had already named as the only one greater. On the extent of his fame Gill, Clarke and Wesley agree in glossing the two towns as the northern and southern limits of the land. Ellicott takes the point further, that the minds of the whole people were thus prepared for the moment when Samuel could be acknowledged as a God-sent chieftain, and quotes the observation that the people, in spite of their disruption, yet formed religiously a unit. Clarke notes that the last verse says God added to appear, meaning that he continued to reveal himself; Gill places this renewed appearing just before the battle with the Philistines that follows.

Clarke closes the chapter by leaving the narrative altogether for an argument about education. Here again, he says, we read of the fearful consequences of a neglected religious upbringing: Eli's sons were wicked, and their father knew the Lord but neither taught his children nor restrained them by his parental authority. Were a proper course pursued in bringing up children, how few profligate sons and daughters and how few broken-hearted parents there would be; the neglect of early religious teaching, joined to a wholesome and affectionate restraint, is the ruin of millions. Then he turns on the excuse parents make for themselves. Many, to cover their indolence and criminal neglect, say that they cannot give their children grace — and what, he asks, do they mean by it, except that God and not they are the author of their children's viciousness? They may shudder at the imputation, but they have not given right precepts, nor brought their children under firm and affectionate restraint, nor shown them by their own temper and conduct how a life should be regulated. Whole nations, he ends, have been corrupted and enfeebled and destroyed through the want of proper education, and parents who neglect it neglect both the present and the eternal interests of their offspring.
